notes: These are newly authored teaching illustrations, not authenticated NSEJS past-paper questions.
All post-attempt worked solutions below are teacher-facing; learner runtime must protect them and retain first-attempt evidence before publication.
No D3/D4 band is assigned. Tasks require shortest-route independent review.

cases.name: Mirror and object both moving
cases.science_conditions: Ideal plane mirror, one-dimensional perpendicular positions measured in one fixed laboratory axis, rays approximated geometrically.
prerequisites: Law of reflection and virtual-image backward extensions

core1a.model: For object at x_o and mirror plane at m, the virtual image coordinate is x_i=2m-x_o by reflection symmetry; therefore Δx_i=2Δm−Δx_o.
core1a.worked_a: An object is stationary at x_o=0 cm and an ideal plane mirror is at m=40 cm. The mirror moves to m=43 cm. Determine the image positions and displacement.
worked_solution: Image displacement is +6 cm even though the mirror moved +3 cm; compare positions in one fixed frame.
core1a.check: The image-to-mirror distance changes from 40 to 43 cm, matching the stationary object's mirror separation.
core1a.misconception: The reflected image always moves the same distance as the mirror. That confuses mirror-plane motion with reflection symmetry.

core1b.original_b: An object at x_o=0 cm and a plane mirror at m=40 cm both move right: the object by 3 cm and the mirror by 4 cm. Find the image's final laboratory coordinate, image displacement, and change in object–image separation.
core1b.protected_work: Combine changes of mirror and object in a fixed coordinate frame, distinguishing image motion from object–image separation.
core1b.predict: Will the image move right by 4 cm, by 8 cm, or by some other distance? Justify qualitatively before calculating.
core1b.attempt: State initial and final x_o and m, derive final x_i and both separations; report signed displacements.
reconstruction: Finally m=44 cm and x_o=3 cm, so x_i=2×44−3=85 cm.
Object–image separation starts at 80 cm and becomes 85−3=82 cm: increase 2 cm.
core1b.diagnose: If the recorded prediction was 8 cm, test whether it used Δx_i=2Δm without accounting for moving object. A different answer requires its own evidence, not an automatic misconception label.
core1b.repair: Draw the original and new mirror planes; place each virtual image by equal signed perpendicular distance rather than memorizing a motion multiplier.
core1b.boundary: If object and mirror translate together by the same displacement, show that image and object translate equally while their mutual separation remains unchanged.

cases.name: Thin-lens conjugate positions: inverse evidence
cases.science_conditions: Ideal thin converging lens with f>0, paraxial rays, fixed real object and screen distance D, real sharp image at the screen, lens located between object and screen.

core1a.model: Let p>0 be object–lens and q=D-p>0 lens–screen. Then pq=fD and p²−Dp+fD=0. Distinct real positions exist only if D>4f, with positions (D±√(D²−4fD))/2.
core1a.worked_a: At fixed object–screen distance D=90 cm, a converging thin lens has f=20 cm. Find the sharp-image positions.
worked_solution: The roots are p=30 and p=60 cm.
The two positions exchange p and q; separation is 30 cm.
At D=4f the two positions coalesce; D<4f has no real in-between lens position under this model.
core1a.check: p+q=90 cm and pq=1800 cm² for either root, so pq=fD.
core1a.misconception: Two algebraic roots are always two distinct usable physical lens positions; the equality and domain cases refute this.

core1b.original_b: A laboratory reports two sharp positions of a thin converging lens 60 cm apart on a fixed 100 cm object–screen track. Determine the focal length and both positions. A classmate then shortens the track to 64 cm and claims there must still be two distinct sharp positions. Evaluate the claim for this same lens.
core1b.protected_work: Infer f from observed conjugate separation, then test a changed track against the discriminant boundary.
core1b.predict: Does shortening the track to 64 cm preserve two distinct positions? State the governing condition before calculation.
core1b.attempt: Derive f=(D²−d²)/(4D), compute positions, and adjudicate the changed-track claim using domain and equality.
reconstruction: On a D=64 cm track, D=4f; the discriminant is zero, giving one position p=q=32 cm.
The classmate's 'two distinct' claim is false.
core1b.diagnose: If two positions were reported at D=64 cm, distinguish 'one double root' from 'two positions' before attributing an algebra error.
core1b.repair: Reconstruct the quadratic and discriminate D>4f, D=4f and D<4f; do not rely on a remembered focal-length formula alone.
core1b.boundary: Under the same lens model, state what changes if D is reduced to 60 cm and why no real sharp screen image position exists.

cases.name: Topology before arithmetic: parallel branches behind a series resistor
cases.science_conditions: Steady DC, ideal 12 V source, ideal wires, ideal ohmic resistors at unchanged temperature, no unintended crossing connections.

core1a.model: Parallel elements share two nodes and thus potential difference. Current splits according to I=V/R; equivalent resistance follows 1/R_p=1/R_1+1/R_2.
core1a.worked_a: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are connected directly in parallel across an ideal 12 V supply. Compute the branch and total currents.
worked_solution: The same 12 V is across each branch.
Total current is 6 A; equivalent resistance is 12/6=2 Ω.
core1a.check: The parallel equivalent must be smaller than the smallest positive branch resistance; 2 Ω < 3 Ω.
core1a.misconception: Nearby components or crossing wires are automatically parallel; topology is determined by connected nodes, not picture proximity.

core1b.original_b: An ideal 12 V battery drives a 2 Ω resistor in series with two resistors, 6 Ω and 3 Ω, connected in parallel after it. Find the total current, voltage across the parallel network and each branch current. A student states each parallel branch receives 12 V because 'parallel resistors get the source voltage.' Check this claim.
core1b.protected_work: Choose a mixed-series/parallel graph, distinguish branch voltage from source voltage, conserve junction current.
core1b.predict: Will either parallel branch receive the full 12 V? Explain qualitatively before computing.
core1b.attempt: Identify nodes, reduce the parallel block, calculate the source current and node-pair voltage, then calculate and check branch currents.
reconstruction: R_total=2+2=4 Ω, so source current=12/4=3 A.
Parallel block voltage=3×2=6 V, not 12 V.
core1b.diagnose: If the saved answer gave 12 V across each branch, investigate whether the learner overlooked the upstream series drop; do not assign that misconception to unrelated incorrect answers.
core1b.repair: Redraw the common nodes and mark the 2 Ω series resistor's 6 V drop before applying the equal-voltage rule within the parallel block.
core1b.boundary: If the upstream 2 Ω resistor is removed and replaced by ideal wire, predict the revised branch currents and explain why the original direct-parallel example applies.

cases.name: Induced emf versus induced current under changing linkage
cases.science_conditions: Conducting loop in a changing magnetic flux configuration; qualitative electromagnetic induction; do not equate an open circuit's induced emf with sustained circulating current.

core1a.model: A change in magnetic flux linkage produces an induced electromotive response; a closed conducting loop permits circulating current if resistance and other conditions allow. A strong stationary field with unchanged linkage does not imply sustained induction.
core1a.worked_a: A bar magnet approaches a stationary closed loop, is held still, and then is withdrawn along the same axis. Predict the qualitative meter response across each stage.
worked_solution: During approach, linkage changes and an induced current can flow.
While magnet and loop are held stationary, linkage is unchanged and the induction response ceases.
During withdrawal, linkage changes oppositely and the current direction reverses relative to approach, with consistent magnet orientation.
core1a.check: Response depends on flux change rather than field strength alone; direction claims require a specified observer and pole.
core1a.misconception: A magnetic field itself causes continuous induction even when flux linkage does not change.

core1b.original_b: A conducting rectangular loop rotates in a uniform constant magnetic field. Initially its area normal is aligned with the field; it rotates until the normal is perpendicular, then stops. Compare (i) a closed loop with finite resistance, (ii) the same loop with a small open gap. Explain the induced emf and whether circulating current can occur during rotation and after it stops.
core1b.protected_work: Recognize that steady B can yield changing linkage through changing orientation; separate induced emf from a closed current path.
core1b.predict: Can a time-independent magnetic field produce an induced electrical response in a rotating loop? Does an open gap change emf, current, or both?
core1b.attempt: Track Φ=B A cosθ qualitatively for the two orientations; state the response in closed and open loop cases during and after rotation.
reconstruction: As θ changes from 0 to 90°, Φ changes from BA to 0 even though B itself is constant.
A nonzero induced emf can arise during rotation; a closed resistive loop can carry circulating current.
With an open gap, an induced voltage can appear but there is no complete path for sustained circulating current.
When orientation stops changing and the field remains static, flux is constant and induced emf ceases in this model.
core1b.diagnose: If the first attempt predicted no induction because B is constant, check whether it omitted orientation-dependent flux. If it predicted current across an open gap, check topology separately.
core1b.repair: Represent the loop with an area-normal arrow and track cosθ and electrical continuity as two independent conditions.
core1b.boundary: If the loop spins about its own area-normal axis with that normal fixed relative to a spatially uniform field, explain why the linked flux stays unchanged in the idealized geometry.
